title: Keeping Up — Claude Code Ships Weekly

questions.prompt: A teammate asks how to keep their own notes from going stale the way yours did. What is the durable instruction?
options: Re-read the docs from the top every few weeks so nothing gets missed
Sort each note into mechanism, surface, or model; date and link the surface ones; re-check them when the version changes
Only write down things you have personally tested, since tested behaviour can't go stale
Copy commands verbatim from the docs so the wording can never be wrong
questions.explanation: The three tiers tell you what to spend attention on: mechanism notes are permanent, model notes should be aliases, and surface notes are the only ones worth a date and a link. Re-checking happens on a version change, not on a calendar. A is the tempting one because it sounds thorough, and it is exactly the job nobody sustains — you either drown or stop, and both leave you trusting undated notes. C fails on precision: something tested and working on one version is the definition of a version-gated claim, not a durable one. D fixes the wording while the command itself moves under it, so the quote stays accurate and the instruction stops working.

questions.prompt: A new release adds a flag and renames a settings key you use. You have a ledger of about forty claims. What does the release actually obligate you to do?
options: Re-verify all forty, since any of them could have changed
Re-check the surface rows, especially the renamed key, and leave the mechanism rows alone
Update the two things you know about and re-check the rest only if something breaks
Nothing — the ledger is a record, and records are corrected when you next read them
questions.explanation: A rename is a surface change, so it invalidates a surface row and nothing else — the loop still loops, the window still fills, the graph is still a graph. That is the payoff of having sorted the claims in the first place. A is the tempting one because a ledger looks like a to-do list, but a changelog entry names its components, so you can diff it against the rows that mention them. C is the opt-in version of the same mistake: 'breaks' is how surface changes present, and you will find out on a teammate's machine. D treats the ledger as archaeology rather than an instrument, which is what makes notes rot silently.

questions.prompt: A hook has run correctly for eight months. Today it fires with a payload shape you didn't expect, and nothing in your repo changed. Where is the fault most likely, and what is the first move?
options: Your repository — something changed the input; bisect the commits
The surface layer — the event's payload changed in a release; check the hooks reference and the changelog for the version
The model — it produced a differently-shaped payload this time
Nothing is wrong; the payload was always like that and you misremembered
questions.explanation: A hook payload is surface: the event fires from the harness, not from your repo and not from the model, so the first suspect is a release that moved the shape. The reference page tells you the current shape; the changelog dates the change and names the version. A is tempting because 'what changed on my side' is the usual debugging instinct, and here your side is unchanged — eight months of stability is evidence the fault is upstream. C misplaces the origin: the harness calls the hook and hands it its arguments. D is the failure mode this whole lesson is about — deciding your memory is right and the system is lying, without opening the page.
